title: Willow Expansion: Trump Opens 82% of Alaska's Petroleum Reserve to Drilling
synopsis: Trump's administration moved on multiple fronts to massively expand oil drilling in Alaska's National Petroleum Reserve, the largest tract of public land in the United States at 23.5 million acres. On December 5, 2025, Trump signed Senate Joint Resolution 80, using the Congressional Review Act to revoke Biden-era 2022 restrictions that had protected ecologically sensitive areas of the NPR-A from drilling. On December 22, 2025, the Bureau of Land Management approved a new management plan opening approximately 82% of the NPR-A to oil and gas leasing — reverting to Trump's 2020 plan and announcing the first lease sale in the reserve since 2019. Separately, in November 2025 the administration fast-tracked ConocoPhillips' winter exploration program near its giant Willow discovery, approving plans for 4 exploratory wells, 60 miles of ice roads, seismic testing across 300 square miles, and the extraction of 90 million gallons of freshwater from Arctic lakes — all with only a one-week public comment period, the first day of which fell on Veterans Day. An Alaska Native group, Sovereign Inu_piat for a Living Arctic, sued to stop the exploration, citing inadequate environmental review and threats to the Teshekpuk caribou herd. Environmental groups warned that Willow's approval as a foot in the door for broader Arctic industrialization had been confirmed.

title: National Forests and BLM Lands Opened to Logging and Mining — 280 Million Acres Targeted
synopsis: On March 1, 2025, Trump signed an executive order titled Immediate Expansion of American Timber Production, directing the Forest Service and BLM to ramp up logging across 280 million acres of federal lands by bypassing Endangered Species Act consultations, creating categorical exclusions from environmental review under NEPA, and setting multi-year timber sale volume targets. title: Trump Bans Offshore Wind — Total Moratorium Issued on His First Day Back in Office
synopsis: On January 20, 2025, Trump signed a presidential memorandum withdrawing all areas of the Outer Continental Shelf from disposition for wind energy leasing indefinitely, effective January 21, halting new offshore wind leases across the entire Atlantic, Pacific, and Gulf coasts, and suspending all federal approvals, permits, rights-of-way, and loans for both offshore and onshore wind projects pending an administration review. The order also targeted a specific Idaho project — the 231-turbine Lava Ridge Wind Project — ordering a moratorium on all activities under its federal permit. Trump justified the anti-wind order by falsely claiming offshore wind turbines caused increases in whale deaths, saying they kill your birds and they ruin your beautiful landscapes, despite no scientific evidence supporting these claims. The moratorium threatened to strand billions of dollars in offshore wind investments by companies including Orsted, Avangrid, and Dominion, and threatened to block the buildout of an energy sector the U.S. had been developing to compete with China and Europe. Analysts warned the indefinite halt would cost tens of thousands of clean energy jobs, raise long-term electricity costs, and cede American leadership in offshore wind technology to foreign competitors at a moment when the industry was nearing commercial viability at scale.

title: WOTUS Gutted — Trump Rule Would Strip Federal Protection From 80% of U.S. Wetlands
synopsis: On November 17, 2025, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and Assistant Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced a proposed rule redefining Waters of the United States under the Clean Water Act that would, according to EPA and Army Corps' own regulatory impact analysis, leave 81% of U.S. wetlands by acreage without federal protection — only about 17.4 million of the roughly 110 million mapped acres in the contiguous United States would retain Clean Water Act coverage. The proposal, posted to the Federal Register on November 20 with a 45-day comment period, built upon the 2023 Supreme Court Sackett v. EPA ruling but adopted an even more restrictive interpretation than Biden's post-Sackett conforming rule, adding requirements that wetlands must hold surface water during the wet season to qualify. In Arizona, just 2.4% of wetlands would be covered; in Iowa, only 5%. Zeldin framed the rule as putting a dagger through the heart of climate change religion, while farm bureaus and real estate developers praised it as ending federal overreach. Environmentalists called it a giveaway to developers, ranchers, and industry that would accelerate the loss of wetlands that filter drinking water, provide flood mitigation, and sustain endangered wildlife — at a moment when the U.S. has already lost more than half its original wetland acreage since European settlement.

title: Trump Guts Wildfire Prevention Funding Weeks After Los Angeles Burns
synopsis: In the weeks immediately following the January 2025 Los Angeles wildfires — expected to be the costliest in U.S. history with losses potentially reaching $35 billion — the Trump administration froze wildfire prevention funding, fired thousands of firefighting-adjacent personnel, and halted seasonal firefighter hiring across the country. By February 13-14, 2025, reports confirmed that the administration had frozen all remaining funds from the $3 billion in wildfire mitigation money appropriated through the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and Inflation Reduction Act, canceling contracts with non-profits like the Oregon-based Lomakatsi Restoration Project. On February 15, 2025, the New York Times reported that 3,400 U.S. Forest Service employees — roughly 10% of the agency's workforce — had been terminated, eliminating trail crews, fuel-reduction specialists, and training instructors who form the backbone of wildfire preparedness. A planned 151,434-acre prescribed burn in Everglades National Park was canceled; training programs for forest firefighters were scrapped mid-season; and seasonal hiring stalled just as fire season approached. Federal firefighters told ProPublica that it's always cheaper to do a prescribed burn than to fight an escaped wildfire, while the annual area burned by U.S. wildfires over the past decade was already 43% larger than the historical average tracked since 1983.
